newsitem.title: UK: Dollar ends below 1.72 marks in late Europe.
newsitem.headline: Dollar ends below 1.72 marks in late Europe.

text.p: The dollar motored back to 34-month highs after a hefty rise in U.S non-farm payrolls and a fall in the jobless rate, but settled off peaks in Europe as the figures failed to convince the market of an imminent rate hike.

"The employment numbers are pretty good...On the other hand, they are not strong enough to give the market a view the Fed will be definitely be tightening rates," said Tony Norfield, treasury economist at ABN AMR0.
At 1628 the dollar stood at 1.7182/92 marks after spiking briefly to session peaks of 1.7210 marks, also a 34-month high.

It was still up, however, against 1.7158/63 in late Europe on Thursday. Against the yen, the dollar climbed to session peaks at 122.12 but retrenched later to stand at 121.92/1.97, though still up from 121.14/90 yen in late Europe on Thursday.
The dollar's brief jolt up came as February non-farm payrolls rose a huge 339,000 against a revised 247,000 jump in January and well-above forecasts for growth of 230,000.
The February jobless rate slipped to 5.3 percent against 5.4 percent in January and average hourly earnings rose slightly to $12.09 from $12.06 in January.

U.S. Treasury bond prices recovered to trade higher on Friday after a near one-point drop following the data and Wall Street stocks opened higher as both bond and asset markets focused on timid wage inflation figures.
"It's a big number on growth, but there are no big-time numbers on inflation," said Robert Dederick, consulting economist at Northern Trust.

Analysts said that while non-farm payrolls and jobless numbers were robust in February, downward revisions to the December and January payroll figures as well as an upwards bias in the February construction numbers were diluting the report.
January and December payrolls growth were revised lower on Friday, by 24,000 and 30,000, respectively.

"The fact you have these revisions for December and January, clearly, does take out some of the sting of it, and the construction sector looks very strong," said Brian Hilliard, chief international economist at Society Generale Strauss Turnbull.
"But construction is not the only sector that is strong...Whichever way you cut it, the labour market is still strengthening," Hilliard added.
Hilliard also said markets should pay more attention to a longer working week in the U.S., more overtime hours and some strength in earnings growth.
"And in the context of Mr. (Alan) Greenspan's Humphrey-Hawkins testimony, that has to keep him alert to potential inflation pressures," he added.
Greenspan said on Tuesday it was crucial to keep inflation down.
The dollar's retrenchment from session highs at 1.7210 marks on Friday also came from profit-taking on positions built-up in anticipation of a strong figure, said traders.
But analysts said the dollar has potential to go higher after its brief lull.
"You still have this favourable scenario for the U.S...We are still bullish on the dollar," said ABN AMRO's Norfield.
